concepts: Section formula and convex combination of complex numbers
questions.question: Let $z_1,z_2,z_3$ be three pairwise distinct complex numbers and $t_1,t_2,t_3$ non-negative real numbers such that $t_1+t_2+t_3=1$. Prove that the complex number $z=t_1z_1+t_2z_2+t_3z_3$ lies inside the triangle with vertices $z_1,z_2,z_3$ or on its boundary.
questions.key_idea: Apply the section formula twice: $D$ on $BC$, then $E$ on $AD$ gives exactly $z=\sum t_kz_k$.
solution: Let $A,B,C$ be the points $z_1,z_2,z_3$. We show that $z=t_1z_1+t_2z_2+t_3z_3$ with $t_k\ge0$, $\sum t_k=1$ lies in or on $\triangle ABC$.
If $t_2+t_3=0$ then $t_2=t_3=0$, $t_1=1$ and $z=z_1$, a vertex. Otherwise let $D$ divide $BC$ internally in the ratio $t_3:t_2$; $D$ lies on segment $BC$.
By the section formula the affix of $D$ is $\frac{t_2z_2+t_3z_3}{t_2+t_3}$.
Let $E$ divide $AD$ internally in the ratio $(t_2+t_3):t_1$, so $E$ lies on segment $AD$ joining a vertex to a point of the opposite side; hence $E$ is in or on the triangle.
Since $t_1+t_2+t_3=1$, this is exactly $z$. So $z=E$ lies inside the triangle or on its boundary. $\blacksquare$
questions.correction_note: The PDF never says that A, B, C denote z1, z2, z3 and it ignores the degenerate case t2+t3=0 (then D is undefined and z is the vertex z1). Both were added; the argument itself is the PDF's.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use barycentric (affine) coordinates: $z=z_1+t_2(z_2-z_1)+t_3(z_3-z_1)$ with $t_2,t_3\ge0$, $t_2+t_3\le1$ describes the filled triangle.
solution: The vertices form a triangle, so $z_2-z_1$ and $z_3-z_1$ are not parallel; every point of the plane is $w=z_1+\lambda(z_2-z_1)+\mu(z_3-z_1)$ for a unique pair of reals $(\lambda,\mu)$.
The closed triangular region is exactly the set of points with $\lambda\ge0,\ \mu\ge0,\ \lambda+\mu\le1$ (the sides are $\lambda=0$, $\mu=0$, $\lambda+\mu=1$).
Hence $z$ lies in the closed triangle; it is interior when all $t_k>0$ and on the boundary when some $t_k=0$.

useful_results: $z=\sum t_kz_k$ with $t_k\ge0$, $\sum t_k=1$ describes exactly the convex hull of the points $z_k$; for three non-collinear points it is the filled triangle (all $t_k>0$: interior; some $t_k=0$: boundary).
Section formula: the point dividing $z_1,z_2$ internally in the ratio $m:n$ is $\frac{nz_1+mz_2}{m+n}$. Nesting it twice proves barycentric statements such as the concurrency of medians.
Special cases: $t_1=t_2=t_3=\frac13$ gives the centroid; $t_1=0$ gives a point of side $BC$; $t_2=t_3=0$ gives the vertex $A$.

concepts: Properties and expansion of determinants
Euler's form of a complex number
questions.question: If $A,B,C$ are the angles of a triangle, find the value of $D=\left|\begin{matrix} e^{-2iA} & e^{iC} & e^{iB}\\ e^{iC} & e^{-2iB} & e^{iA}\\ e^{iB} & e^{iA} & e^{-2iC}\end{matrix}\right|$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$.
questions.key_idea: After expanding, every term collapses to a power of $e^{i(A+B+C)}=e^{i\pi}=-1$.
solution: Since $A,B,C$ are angles of a triangle, $A+B+C=\pi$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Scale rows to get $2I-N$ with $N$ of rank one; its eigenvalues are $3,0,0$, so $\det(2I-N)=(2-3)\cdot2\cdot2$.
solution: Multiply rows 1, 2, 3 by $p^2,q^2,r^2$: the determinant gets multiplied by $p^2q^2r^2=1$, so $D$ is unchanged.

Row 1 becomes $(1,\ p^2r,\ p^2q)$. Using $pr=-\frac1q$ and $pq=-\frac1r$ this is $\left(1,\ -\frac pq,\ -\frac pr\right)$; likewise rows 2, 3 are $\left(-\frac qp,\ 1,\ -\frac qr\right)$ and $\left(-\frac rp,\ -\frac rq,\ 1\right)$.
So the matrix is $2I-N$ where $N_{jk}=\frac{v_j}{v_k}$ with $v=(p,q,r)$: all diagonal entries of $N$ are $1$ and $2I-N$ has diagonal $2-1=1$.
$N=v\,w^{T}$ with $w=\left(\frac1p,\frac1q,\frac1r\right)$ has rank one; its eigenvalues are $w^{T}v=3$ and $0,0$.

useful_results: For a triangle $A+B+C=\pi$, so $e^{i(A+B+C)}=-1$ and $e^{2i(A+B+C)}=1$; products such as $e^{-2iA}e^{-2i(B+C)}$ collapse at once.
A matrix $aI+uv^{T}$ (rank-one perturbation of a scalar matrix) has $\det=a^{n-1}\left(a+v^{T}u\right)$ - here $2I-vw^T$ gives $2^2(2-3)=-4$.
Multiplying row $j$ by $x_j$ multiplies the determinant by $x_j$; scaling by powers of $e^{i\theta}$ often reveals a symmetric structure.

concepts: Cube roots of unity and polar form of complex numbers
questions.question: If $x=1+i\sqrt3$, $y=1-i\sqrt3$ and $z=2$, prove that $x^p+y^p=z^p$ for every prime $p>3$.
questions.key_idea: $\frac x2=-\omega^2$ and $\frac y2=-\omega$, and $\omega^p+\omega^{2p}=-1$ whenever $3\nmid p$.
solution: Divide by $z^p=2^p$: we must show $\left(\frac xz\right)^p+\left(\frac yz\right)^p=1$.
So the left side is $(-\omega^2)^p+(-\omega)^p=-\left(\omega^{2p}+\omega^{p}\right)$, because $p$ is odd.
A prime $p>3$ is not a multiple of $3$, so $\omega^p$ is $\omega$ or $\omega^2$ and $\{\omega^p,\omega^{2p}\}=\{\omega,\omega^2\}$.
Hence $1+\omega^p+\omega^{2p}=1+\omega+\omega^2=0$, so the left side is $1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $x,y$ in polar form: $x^p+y^p=2^{p+1}\cos\frac{p\pi}{3}$, and primes $>3$ are $\equiv\pm1\pmod 6$.
solution: A prime $p>3$ is odd and not divisible by $3$, so $p\equiv\pm1\pmod 6$, i.e. $p=6m\pm1$.

useful_results: $1+\omega^k+\omega^{2k}=0$ if $3\nmid k$ and $=3$ if $3\mid k$.
$(1\pm i\sqrt3)^n=2^ne^{\pm in\pi/3}$, so $x^n+y^n=2^{n+1}\cos\frac{n\pi}3$; this equals $2^n$ iff $n\equiv\pm1\pmod 6$.
Every prime $p>3$ satisfies $p\equiv\pm1\pmod6$; this reduces many questions on primes to two residue cases.
For conjugates $x,\bar x$: $x^n+\bar x^n=2\,\mathrm{Re}(x^n)$ is always real.

concepts: Triangle inequality for complex numbers
Sum of an infinite geometric series
questions.question: Prove that there exists no complex number $z$ with $|z|<\frac13$ and $\sum_{r=1}^{n}a_rz^r=1$, where $|a_r|<2$.
questions.key_idea: Bound $\left|\sum a_rz^r\right|$ by a geometric series; it forces $|z|>\frac13$ - contradiction.
solution: Suppose such a $z$ exists. Then $1=\left|\sum a_rz^r\right|\le\sum|a_r||z|^r$ (triangle inequality).
Case I, $|z|<1$: the finite sum is less than the infinite series, so $\frac1{1-|z|}>\frac32$, i.e. $2>3-3|z|$.
Case II, $|z|\ge1$: then $|z|<\frac13$ is false at once.
In both cases $|z|<\frac13$ and $\sum a_rz^r=1$ cannot hold together. $\blacksquare$

alternate_solutions.idea: Bound directly: for $t=|z|<\frac13$, $\frac{t}{1-t}<\frac12$, so $\left|\sum a_rz^r\right|<2\cdot\frac12=1$.
solution: Take $0<|z|<\frac13$ (for $z=0$ the sum is $0\ne1$) and let $t=|z|$.
For $0<t<1$ the finite sum is less than the infinite series: $t+\dots+t^n<\frac{t}{1-t}$.
The function $\frac t{1-t}$ increases on $(0,1)$ and equals $\frac12$ at $t=\frac13$; so $\frac t{1-t}<\frac12$ when $t<\frac13$.
Hence $\left|\sum a_rz^r\right|<2\cdot\frac12=1$, so the sum can never equal $1$. $\blacksquare$

useful_results: To show a polynomial has no zero in a disc, bound $\left|\sum a_rz^r\right|\le\sum|a_r||z|^r$ and sum the tail as a geometric series.
If $|a_r|\le M$ and $|z|<\frac1{M+1}$ then $\left|\sum_{r\ge1}a_rz^r\right|<1$, because $\frac{Mt}{1-t}<1\iff t<\frac1{M+1}$. Here $M=2$ gives $\frac13$.
For $0<t<1$: $t+t^2+\dots+t^n<\frac t{1-t}$.

concepts: Cube roots of a complex number
questions.question: Let $Z=18+26i$ and let $Z_0=x_0+iy_0$ ($x_0,y_0\in\mathbb R$) be the cube root of $Z$ having the least positive argument. Find the value of $x_0y_0(x_0+y_0)$.
questions.key_idea: The cube root with least positive argument has argument $\frac\theta3$; $\tan\frac\theta3$ solves the triple-angle cubic.
solution: The cube roots are $(10\sqrt{10})^{1/3}e^{i(2k\pi+\theta)/3}$, $k=0,1,2$; the least positive argument is for $k=0$, namely $\frac\theta3$.
Since $\theta<90^\circ$, $\frac\theta3<30^\circ$ and $0<x<\frac1{\sqrt3}$; the other roots of the cubic are $\approx4.9$ and $\approx-0.89$, so $x=\frac13$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the modulus: $|Z_0|^2=\sqrt[3]{|Z|^2}=10$, so look for integers with $x_0^2+y_0^2=10$.
solution: Indeed $(3+i)^3=(8+6i)(3+i)=24+8i+18i-6=18+26i$, so $3+i$ is a cube root of $Z$.
The other cube roots are $(3+i)\omega$ and $(3+i)\omega^2$, with arguments $\arg(3+i)+120^\circ$ and $+240^\circ$; so $3+i$ ($\arg\approx18.4^\circ$) has the least positive argument.

useful_results: The three cube roots of $Z$ are $Z_0,\ Z_0\omega,\ Z_0\omega^2$ with arguments $\frac{\theta}3+\frac{2k\pi}3$; the one with the smallest positive argument has $k=0$.
If $|Z|$ is a perfect cube of a Gaussian-integer norm, try small Gaussian integers: $(1+i)^3=-2+2i$, $(2+i)^3=2+11i$, $(3+i)^3=18+26i$, $(2+3i)^3=-46+9i$.
$\tan3\varphi=\frac{3t-t^3}{1-3t^2}$ with $t=\tan\varphi$: the root in the correct quadrant gives $\tan\frac\theta3$.

concepts: Roots of complex numbers
Binomial theorem for a positive integral index
questions.question: If $\omega$ is the fifth root of $2$ and $x=\omega+\omega^2$, prove that $x^5=10x^2+10x+6$.
questions.key_idea: Factor $x=\omega(1+\omega)$ so that $x^5=\omega^5(1+\omega)^5=2(1+\omega)^5$, then regroup the expansion in powers of $x$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Treat $\omega$ as a variable $t$ and show $t^5-2$ divides $P(t)=(t+t^2)^5-10(t+t^2)^2-10(t+t^2)-6$.
solution: Let $P(t)=(t+t^2)^5-10(t+t^2)^2-10(t+t^2)-6$. We show $P(t)=(t^5-2)\cdot R(t)$; then $P(\omega)=0$ because $\omega^5=2$.

useful_results: If $\omega^n=a$ then $\omega$ is a root of $t^n-a$; any polynomial identity in $\omega$ can be proved by divisibility by $t^n-a$ or by reducing powers with $\omega^n=a$.
Factoring out the lowest power, $\omega+\omega^2=\omega(1+\omega)$, turns a fifth power into $\omega^5(1+\omega)^5=2(1+\omega)^5$.

$x^5-10x^2-10x-6$ is the minimal polynomial of $\omega+\omega^2$ over $\mathbb Q$: it is irreducible by Eisenstein's criterion at $2$ (coefficients $10,10,6$ divisible by $2$, $6$ not divisible by $4$).

concepts: Algebraic identities for complex numbers and real-valued expressions
questions.question: Let $z_1,z_2\in\mathbb C$ such that $z_1^2+z_2^2\in\mathbb R$. If $z_1(z_1^2-3z_2^2)=10$ and $z_2(3z_1^2-z_2^2)=30$, find the value of $z_1^2+z_2^2$.
questions.key_idea: $z_1^3-3z_1z_2^2+i\left(3z_1^2z_2-z_2^3\right)=(z_1+iz_2)^3$; multiplying it by its partner gives $(z_1^2+z_2^2)^3$.
solution: Multiply the second by $i$ and add: $z_1^3-3z_1z_2^2+3iz_1^2z_2-iz_2^3=10+30i$.
Multiply the second equation by $-i$ and add: $(z_1-iz_2)^3=10-30i$ ... (B).
$z_1^2+z_2^2$ is real and the only real cube root of $1000$ is $10$, so $z_1^2+z_2^2=10$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the polynomial identity $(a^2+b^2)^3=(a^3-3ab^2)^2+(3a^2b-b^3)^2$ - no complex multiplication needed.
solution: $z_1^2+z_2^2$ is real, so it is the real cube root of $1000$.

useful_results: For real $x,y$: $x^3-3xy^2=\mathrm{Re}(x+iy)^3$ and $3x^2y-y^3=\mathrm{Im}(x+iy)^3$ (the $\cos3\theta,\sin3\theta$ patterns).
Identity: $(a^2+b^2)^3=(a^3-3ab^2)^2+(3a^2b-b^3)^2$ ($|w^3|=|w|^3$ for $w=a+ib$); it holds for complex $a,b$ as a polynomial identity.
The hypothesis $z_1^2+z_2^2\in\mathbb R$ selects the real cube root: otherwise $10,\ 10\omega,\ 10\omega^2$ would all be possible.

concepts: Locus $|z-z_1|=|z-z_2|$ and real and imaginary parts of roots
Relations between roots and coefficients
questions.question: If the equation $(z+1)^7+z^7=0$ has roots $z_1,z_2,\dots,z_7$, find the value of (a) $\sum_{r=1}^{7}\mathrm{Re}(z_r)$ and (b) $\sum_{r=1}^{7}\mathrm{Im}(z_r)$.
questions.key_idea: $(z+1)^7=-z^7$ forces $|z+1|=|z|$, so every root lies on the line $x=-\frac12$.
solution: So $z$ is equidistant from $(0,0)$ and $(-1,0)$ and lies on the perpendicular bisector $x=-\frac12$.
Hence all seven roots have real part $-\frac12$, and $\sum\mathrm{Re}(z_r)=7\cdot\left(-\frac12\right)=-\frac72$.
The equation is $2z^7+7z^6+\dots=0$, so by Vieta $z_1+z_2+\dots+z_7=-\frac72$, a real number.

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve explicitly: $\frac{z+1}{z}$ is a 7th root of $-1$, giving $z=-\frac12-\frac i2\cot\frac\alpha2$.
solution: Each root has real part $-\frac12$, so $\sum\mathrm{Re}\,z_k=-\frac72$.
The imaginary parts are $-\frac12\cot\frac{(2k+1)\pi}{14}$; the terms for $k$ and $6-k$ are $\cot\vartheta$ and $\cot(\pi-\vartheta)=-\cot\vartheta$, which cancel in pairs.

useful_results: $|z-a|=|z-b|$ is the perpendicular bisector of $a,b$; here $|z+1|=|z|$ gives the line $x=-\frac12$.
For $\left(\frac{z+1}{z}\right)^n=\pm1$ all roots lie on $\mathrm{Re}\,z=-\frac12$, and $\frac1{e^{i\alpha}-1}=-\frac12-\frac i2\cot\frac\alpha2$.
A real polynomial has $\sum\mathrm{Im}(z_r)=0$ automatically (conjugate pairs), so only the real part needs work; for $az^n+bz^{n-1}+\dots$ the sum of the roots is $-\frac ba$.

concepts: Roots of unity and factorisation over the reals
Exact values of trigonometric ratios of $18^\circ$ and $36^\circ$
questions.question: If $z^5-32$ is factorised into linear and quadratic factors over real coefficients as $z^5-32=(z-2)(z^2-pz+4)(z^2-qz+4)$, find the value of $p^2+2p$.
questions.key_idea: Pair the conjugate roots: $\left(z-2e^{i\theta}\right)\left(z-2e^{-i\theta}\right)=z^2-4z\cos\theta+4$, so $p=4\cos72^\circ$.
solution: Pairing conjugate roots: $z^5-32=(z-2)\left(z-2e^{2\pi i/5}\right)\left(z-2e^{-2\pi i/5}\right)\left(z-2e^{4\pi i/5}\right)\left(z-2e^{-4\pi i/5}\right)$.
So $p=2\left(e^{2\pi i/5}+e^{-2\pi i/5}\right)=4\cos\frac{2\pi}5$ and $q=4\cos\frac{4\pi}5$ (the two factors are interchangeable; the final value is the same for $q$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Compare coefficients: $\frac{z^5-32}{z-2}=z^4+2z^3+4z^2+8z+16$ forces $p+q=-2$, $pq=-4$, so $p^2+2p-4=0$.
solution: So $p+q=-2$ and $pq=-4$: $p$ and $q$ are the roots of $t^2+2t-4=0$.
Hence $p^2+2p-4=0$, i.e. $p^2+2p=4$ (and the same for $q$) - no trigonometry needed.

useful_results: $z^n-a^n$ factors over $\mathbb R$ into $(z-a)$ and quadratics $z^2-2a\cos\frac{2k\pi}nz+a^2$, $k=1,\dots,\frac{n-1}2$ for odd $n$.
Comparing coefficients with $z^4+2z^3+4z^2+8z+16$ gives $\cos72^\circ+\cos144^\circ=-\frac12$ and $\cos72^\circ\cos144^\circ=-\frac14$.
Exact values: $\cos36^\circ=\frac{\sqrt5+1}4$, $\sin18^\circ=\cos72^\circ=\frac{\sqrt5-1}4$.

concepts: Complex numbers as points in the Argand plane
Square inscribed in a triangle (coordinate geometry)
questions.question: Let $z_i$ ($i=1,2,3,4$) represent the vertices of a square, all of which lie on the sides of the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(2,1)$ and $(3,0)$. If $z_1$ and $z_2$ are purely real, then the area of the triangle formed by $z_3$, $z_4$ and the origin is $\frac mn$ (lowest terms). Find $m+n$.
questions.key_idea: Two real vertices put one side of the square on the base; the vertex heights and the side length give two linear equations.
solution: The triangle is $O(0,0)$, $A(2,1)$, $B(3,0)$. Line $OA$: $y=\frac x2$; line $AB$: $y=3-x$.
$z_1,z_2$ are real, so they are on the side $OB$ of the triangle; the square stands on $OB$. Let $z_1=(a,0)$, $z_2=(b,0)$, $b>a$.
The upper vertices are $z_4=P\left(a,\frac a2\right)$ on $OA$ and $z_3=Q(b,\,3-b)$ on $AB$.
$PQ$ is horizontal, so the two heights are equal: $3-b=\frac a2$ ... (1).
Side length: $b-a=\frac a2$ (the height of $P$), so $2b=3a$ ... (2).
Solving (1),(2): $3-\frac{3a}2=\frac a2$, so $a=\frac32$, $b=\frac94$ and the side is $\frac34$.
Area of $\triangle Oz_3z_4=\frac12\cdot\frac34\cdot\frac34=\frac9{32}$ (base $z_3z_4=\frac34$, height from $O$ to the line $y=\frac34$ is $\frac34$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Similar triangles give the side directly: the small triangle above the square is similar to the whole, so $\frac s3=\frac{1-s}1$.
solution: The square of side $s$ stands on the base $OB=3$; the triangle's height is $1$ (from $A(2,1)$).
The part above the square is similar to the whole triangle, with base $s$ and height $1-s$: $\frac s3=\frac{1-s}{1}$.
So $z_3z_4$ is the horizontal top side of length $\frac34$ at height $\frac34$.

useful_results: The largest square with a side on the base $b$ of a triangle of height $h$ has side $\frac{bh}{b+h}$ (here $\frac{3\cdot1}{3+1}=\frac34$).
Triangle with a vertex at $O$ and base on a horizontal line $y=h$ has area $\frac12\cdot\text{base}\cdot h$, whatever the abscissae of the base endpoints.
Two real vertices of a square inscribed in a triangle lie on the same side of the triangle (a diagonal along that side would put a vertex outside).

concepts: Cube roots of unity
Sums of binomial coefficients using roots of unity
questions.question:
(i) Let $C_r$ denote the binomial coefficients in the expansion of $(1+x)^n$, $n\in\mathbb N$. If the integers $a_n=C_0+C_3+C_6+C_9+\dots$, $b_n=C_1+C_4+C_7+C_{10}+\dots$ and $c_n=C_2+C_5+C_8+C_{11}+\dots$, prove that (a) $a_n^3+b_n^3+c_n^3-3a_nb_nc_n=2^n$, (b) $(a_n-b_n)^2+(b_n-c_n)^2+(c_n-a_n)^2=2$.
(ii) Prove the identity $(C_0-C_2+C_4-C_6+\dots)^2+(C_1-C_3+C_5-C_7+\dots)^2=2^n$.
questions.key_idea: Evaluate $(1+x)^n$ at $1,\omega,\omega^2$ to get $a_n,b_n,c_n$, and use $a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc=(a+b+c)(a+b\omega+c\omega^2)(a+b\omega^2+c\omega)$.
solution: Add (1), (2), (3): the coefficient of $C_r$ is $1+\omega^r+\omega^{2r}$, which is $3$ if $3\mid r$ and $0$ otherwise; so $a_n=\frac{2^n+(-\omega^2)^n+(-\omega)^n}3$.
(b) Also $a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc=(a+b+c)\cdot\frac12\left[(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2\right]$. With $a_n+b_n+c_n=2^n$ and the value $2^n$ from (a): $2^n=2^n\cdot\frac12\left[\dots\right]$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF solves only (i)(a) and (i)(b); part (ii) is missing. Added: put x=i in (1+x)^n and take the squared modulus, |1+i|^(2n)=2^n. Parts (a) and (b) are the PDF's, with the three combinations (a+b+c), (a+b w+c w^2), (a+b w^2+c w) spelled out.

alternate_solutions.idea: Read $a_n+b_n\omega+c_n\omega^2$ directly as $\sum C_r\omega^r=(1+\omega)^n$ - no need to find $a_n,b_n,c_n$.
solution: $\omega^r$ depends only on $r\bmod3$, so $a_n+b_n\omega+c_n\omega^2=\sum C_r\omega^r=(1+\omega)^n$; similarly $a_n+b_n\omega^2+c_n\omega=(1+\omega^2)^n$ and $a_n+b_n+c_n=2^n$.

useful_results: Roots-of-unity filter: $\sum_{r\equiv s\,(\mathrm{mod}\ m)}C_r=\frac1m\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\varepsilon^{-js}\left(1+\varepsilon^{j}\right)^n$ with $\varepsilon=e^{2\pi i/m}$.
$a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc=(a+b+c)(a+b\omega+c\omega^2)(a+b\omega^2+c\omega)$ and $a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca=\left|a+b\omega+c\omega^2\right|^2$ for real $a,b,c$.
Real and imaginary parts of $(1+i)^n$ are the alternating sums $C_0-C_2+\dots$ and $C_1-C_3+\dots$; their squares add to $|1+i|^{2n}=2^n$.

concepts: Rotation of a complex number (vertices of a square)
questions.question: Let $z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4$ be the vertices $A,B,C,D$ respectively of a square on the Argand diagram taken in anticlockwise direction. Prove that (i) $2z_2=(1+i)z_1+(1-i)z_3$ and (ii) $2z_4=(1-i)z_1+(1+i)z_3$.
questions.key_idea: Each side is the previous side rotated by $90^\circ$ anticlockwise: multiply by $e^{i\pi/2}=i$.
solution: (i) In the anticlockwise square, side $BC$ is side $AB$ turned through $90^\circ$ with the same length: $z_3-z_2=(z_2-z_1)e^{i\pi/2}=(z_2-z_1)i$.
(ii) Side $AD$ is side $AB$ turned through $90^\circ$ anticlockwise: $z_4-z_1=(z_2-z_1)i$, so $z_4=iz_2+(1-i)z_1$ ... (1).
Opposite sides $AB$ and $DC$ are equal and parallel: $z_2-z_1=z_3-z_4$, so $z_2=z_3-z_4+z_1$ ... (2).

alternate_solutions.idea: Rotate about the centre: the diagonals bisect each other at $m=\frac{z_1+z_3}2$ and $z_2-m=i(z_1-m)$.
solution: The diagonals of a square bisect each other: centre $m=\frac{z_1+z_3}2=\frac{z_2+z_4}2$.
A rotation of $90^\circ$ anticlockwise about $m$ takes $A\to B$: $z_2-m=i(z_1-m)$, so $z_2=(1-i)m+iz_1$.
Likewise $D$ is $A$ rotated by $-90^\circ$ about $m$: $z_4-m=-i(z_1-m)$, so $z_4=(1+i)m-iz_1$.

useful_results: Rotation by $90^\circ$ anticlockwise about $c$: $w-c=i(z-c)$; by $-90^\circ$: $w-c=-i(z-c)$.
Given a diagonal $z_1,z_3$ of a square, the other vertices are $\frac{(1\pm i)z_1+(1\mp i)z_3}2$.
In a square (or parallelogram) opposite vertices have the same midpoint: $z_1+z_3=z_2+z_4$.

concepts: De Moivre's theorem
Binomial theorem: trigonometric sums
questions.question:
Prove that
(a) $\cos x+{}^nC_1\cos2x+{}^nC_2\cos3x+\dots+{}^nC_n\cos(n+1)x=2^n\cos^n\frac x2\cos\left(\frac{n+2}2\right)x$
(b) $\sin x+{}^nC_1\sin2x+{}^nC_2\sin3x+\dots+{}^nC_n\sin(n+1)x=2^n\cos^n\frac x2\sin\left(\frac{n+2}2\right)x$
questions.key_idea: $1+e^{i\theta}=2\cos\frac\theta2\,e^{i\theta/2}$: factor out the half-angle phase and read off real and imaginary parts.
solution: Equate real and imaginary parts with (*) and put $\theta=x$: the real part gives (a), the imaginary part gives (b). $\blacksquare$
questions.correction_note: The PDF stops at 2^n cos^n(theta/2) e^{i theta (n/2+1)} and never equates real and imaginary parts to obtain (a) and (b). The final step was added; everything before it is the PDF's.
useful_results: $1+e^{i\theta}=2\cos\frac\theta2\,e^{i\theta/2}$ and $1-e^{i\theta}=-2i\sin\frac\theta2\,e^{i\theta/2}$: factor out the half-angle phase to get a real modulus.
Without the extra factor $e^{i\theta}$: $\sum{}^nC_k\cos k\theta=2^n\cos^n\frac\theta2\cos\frac{n\theta}2$ and $\sum{}^nC_k\sin k\theta=2^n\cos^n\frac\theta2\sin\frac{n\theta}2$.
Alternating version: $\sum(-1)^k{}^nC_k\cos k\theta=\left(2\sin\frac\theta2\right)^n\cos\frac{n(\theta-\pi)}2$ (from $1-e^{i\theta}$).
Check $n=1$: $\cos x+\cos2x=2\cos\frac x2\cos\frac{3x}2$, the sum-to-product formula.

concepts: Conjugate roots of a polynomial with real coefficients
Relations between roots and coefficients
questions.question: Let $f(x)=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ be a cubic polynomial with real coefficients satisfying $f(i)=0$ and $f(1+i)=5$. Find the value of $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$.
questions.key_idea: Real coefficients and $f(i)=0$ give the factor $x^2+1$; the third root is real and the imaginary part of $f(1+i)=5$ fixes it.
solution: $f$ has real coefficients and $f(i)=0$, so $f(-i)=0$ too; let the third root be $\alpha$ (it is real, as non-real roots occur in pairs).

alternate_solutions.idea: Real and imaginary parts of $f(i)=0$ give $c=a$, $d=b$ at once; then $f(1+i)=5$ gives two linear equations.
solution: Set this equal to $5$: real part $-a+b=5$, imaginary part $3a+2b=0$.
Solving: $a=-2$, $b=3$, so the required sum is $2(4+9)=26$.

useful_results: A real polynomial vanishing at $i$ is divisible by $x^2+1$; if it vanishes at a non-real $\alpha$, then $x^2-2\mathrm{Re}(\alpha)x+|\alpha|^2$ divides it.
For real coefficients, $f(i)=0$ splits into real and imaginary parts: for a cubic, $d=b$ and $c=a$ (even coefficients equal, odd coefficients equal).
A real cubic with a non-real root has exactly one real root (the third root is real).

concepts: Circle $|z-z_0|=r$ in the Argand plane and rotation
questions.question: A particle starts to travel from a point $P$ on the curve $C_1:|z-3-4i|=5$, where $|z|$ is maximum. From $P$ the particle moves through an angle $\tan^{-1}\frac13$ in anticlockwise direction on $|z-3-4i|=5$ and reaches the point $Q$. From $Q$ it comes down parallel to the imaginary axis by $2$ units and reaches $R$. Find the complex number corresponding to the point $R$ in the Argand plane.
questions.key_idea: The origin lies on the circle and $P$ is diametrically opposite to it; the angle $\tan^{-1}\frac13$ is turned at the origin, so $OQ$ has slope $3$.
solution: Circle $C_1$: centre $C(3,4)$, radius $5$; it passes through the origin since $|0-3-4i|=5$.
$|z|$ is largest at the end of the diameter through the origin: $P=2(3+4i)=6+8i$, with $|OP|=10$.
The direction of $OP$ makes angle $\alpha$ with the real axis, $\tan\alpha=\frac43$.

The particle goes anticlockwise until $OQ$ has turned through $\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac13$ from $OP$ (angle measured at the origin, which lies on the circle - the reading under which the printed answer arises).
$x=0$ is the origin itself (not a new point); so $x=3$, $y=9$ and $Q=3+9i$.
Coming down $2$ units parallel to the imaginary axis: $R=3+9i-2i=3+7i$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF does not say at which point the angle tan^-1(1/3) is measured; its working (line y=3x through the origin) uses the angle at the origin O, which lies on the circle. If the angle were the central angle at C(3,4), Q would be 3+sqrt(10)/2 + i(4+3 sqrt(10)/2), a non-nice point that does not match the printed key 3+7i. The key is kept; the assumption is now stated, and the rejection of the root x=0 (the origin) is written out.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the polar equation of a circle through the origin: a point at polar angle $\phi$ has $|OQ|=10\cos(\phi-\alpha)$.
solution: $OP$ is a diameter of length $10$ in direction $\alpha$, where $\cos\alpha=\frac35$, $\sin\alpha=\frac45$.
A point $Q$ of the circle at polar angle $\phi$ has $|OQ|=10\cos(\phi-\alpha)$, because $\angle OQP=90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle).

useful_results: A circle through the origin with centre $c$ has polar equation $|z|=2|c|\cos(\arg z-\arg c)$; the point farthest from $O$ is $2c$.
Farthest and nearest points of $|z-c|=r$ from the origin are $c\pm r\frac{c}{|c|}$ (distances $|c|\pm r$).
Inscribed angle theorem: an angle at a point of the circle is half the central angle on the same arc (here $\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac13$ at $O$ is a central angle of about $36.9^\circ$ at $C$).
Unit complex numbers from Pythagorean triples: $\frac{3+4i}5$ and $\frac{3+i}{\sqrt{10}}$ multiply without square roots.

concepts: Sum of roots of unity
Arithmetico-geometric series
questions.question: Evaluate $\sum_{p=1}^{32}(3p+2)\left(\sum_{q=1}^{10}\left(\sin\frac{2q\pi}{11}-i\cos\frac{2q\pi}{11}\right)\right)^p$.
questions.key_idea: $\sin x-i\cos x=-ie^{ix}$ and the roots of unity sum to $-1$ (without $1$), so the inner sum is $i$; the outer sum is a series in $i^p$.

alternate_solutions.idea: After the inner sum $=i$, group the terms $p=4m+1,\dots,4m+4$: each block of four contributes the same $6(1-i)$.
solution: The inner sum is $i$ (as above), so we need $\sum_{p=1}^{32}(3p+2)i^p$.
The powers $i^p$ repeat with period $4$: $i,-1,-i,1$ for $p=4m+1,4m+2,4m+3,4m+4$.
There are $8$ blocks ($p=1,\dots,32$), so the sum is $8\cdot6(1-i)=48(1-i)$.

useful_results: $\cos x+i\sin x=e^{ix}$, $\sin x-i\cos x=-ie^{ix}$, $\sin x+i\cos x=ie^{-ix}$.
$\sum_{q=1}^{n-1}e^{2\pi iq/n}=-1$, i.e. $\sum\cos\frac{2\pi q}n=-1$ and $\sum\sin\frac{2\pi q}n=0$.
For $\sum p\,x^p$ use $S-xS$ (arithmetico-geometric); at $x=i$ the period is $4$, and a full block $\sum_{p=4m+1}^{4m+4}(3p+2)i^p=6(1-i)$ is independent of $m$.

concepts: Roots of unity in a cyclic system of equations
questions.question: Let $a,b,c$ be distinct complex numbers such that $\frac a{1-b}=\frac b{1-c}=\frac c{1-a}=k$. Find the value of $k$.
questions.key_idea: Eliminate $b$ and $c$ to get $(k^2-k+1)(ak+a-k)=0$; distinctness of $a,b,c$ kills the second factor.
solution: Starting the elimination from $b$ or $c$ gives in the same way $(k^2-k+1)(bk+b-k)=0$ and $(k^2-k+1)(ck+c-k)=0$.
If $k^2-k+1\ne0$ then $a(k+1)=b(k+1)=c(k+1)=k$; $k=-1$ would give $0=-1$, so $k\ne-1$ and $a=b=c=\frac k{k+1}$, contradicting distinctness.
questions.correction_note: The PDF dismisses the factor k = a/(1-a) with the bare words 'is not possible'. The reason (the same elimination from b and c would force a=b=c, contradicting distinctness) was added; the printed ending 'Hence Proved' is irrelevant to this find-k question.

alternate_solutions.idea: The equations are linear in $a,b,c$: the coefficient determinant is $1+k^3$, and a unique solution would be $a=b=c$.
solution: If $1+k^3\ne0$ the solution is unique, and $a=b=c=\frac k{1+k}$ is one (valid for $k\ne-1$) - contradicting distinctness; and $k=-1$ is inconsistent (adding the equations gives $0=-3$).

These values do occur: then the system has a line of solutions $a=\frac k{1+k}+t$, $b=\frac k{1+k}-\frac tk$, $c=\frac k{1+k}+\frac t{k^2}$ with $t\ne0$, and $1,\ -\frac1k,\ \frac1{k^2}$ are pairwise distinct, so $a,b,c$ are distinct.

useful_results: Cyclic systems $a=f(b)$, $b=f(c)$, $c=f(a)$ are solved by composing three times, or - when $f$ is linear - as a linear system with a circulant determinant, here $1+k^3$.
Distinctness of the unknowns is typically used to discard the symmetric solution $a=b=c$.
$k^2-k+1=0\iff k=e^{\pm i\pi/3}=-\omega^{2},-\omega$ (primitive sixth roots of unity), and $k^3=-1$.

concepts: Locus of a point in the Argand plane: circle
questions.question: Let $\alpha,\beta$ be fixed complex numbers and $z$ a variable complex number such that $|z-\alpha|^2+|z-\beta|^2=k$. Find the limits for $k$ such that the locus of $z$ is a circle. Find also the centre and radius of the circle.
questions.key_idea: Expand with $|w|^2=w\bar w$ and compare with $z\bar z-\bar cz-c\bar z+|c|^2-r^2=0$.
solution: A circle with centre $c$ and radius $r$ is $z\bar z-\bar cz-c\bar z+|c|^2-r^2=0$; so the centre is $c=\frac{\alpha+\beta}2$.
A genuine circle needs $r^2>0$: $2k>|\alpha-\beta|^2$, i.e. $k>\frac12|\alpha-\beta|^2$; radius $=\frac12\sqrt{2k-|\alpha-\beta|^2}$ (equality gives the single point $\frac{\alpha+\beta}2$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Apollonius' median theorem: $PA^2+PB^2=2PM^2+\frac12AB^2$, with $M$ the midpoint of $AB$.
solution: Let $A,B$ be the points $\alpha,\beta$, $P$ the point $z$, and $M=\frac{\alpha+\beta}2$ the midpoint of $AB$.
This is a circle with centre $\frac{\alpha+\beta}2$ and radius$^2=\frac k2-\frac{|\alpha-\beta|^2}4=\frac{2k-|\alpha-\beta|^2}4$.
It exists (positive radius) iff $k>\frac12|\alpha-\beta|^2$; at equality it is a point, below it the locus is empty.

useful_results: Apollonius median theorem: $PA^2+PB^2=2PM^2+\frac12AB^2$; so $PA^2+PB^2=k$ is a circle about the midpoint $M$.
$z\bar z+\bar az+a\bar z+b=0$ ($b$ real) is a circle with centre $-a$ and radius $\sqrt{|a|^2-b}$ when $|a|^2>b$.
Special case $k=|\alpha-\beta|^2$: radius $\frac{|\alpha-\beta|}2$, the circle on $AB$ as diameter ($PA^2+PB^2=AB^2$, Pythagoras).

concepts: Roots of unity as vertices of a polygon and its area
questions.question: If the area of the polygon whose vertices are the solutions (in the complex plane) of the equation $x^7+x^6+x^5+x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1=0$ can be expressed in the simplest form as $\frac{a\sqrt b+c}d$, find the value of $a+b+c+d$.
questions.key_idea: $x^7+\dots+1=\frac{1-x^8}{1-x}$: the roots are the 8th roots of unity except $1$, a regular octagon with one vertex missing.
solution: The roots are $x=e^{2ik\pi/8}$, $k=1,2,\dots,7$: the 8th roots of unity except $1$, on the unit circle at $45^\circ$ spacing.
The polygon has these $7$ vertices; join the origin to each. Between consecutive vertices ($k=1$ to $7$) there are $6$ triangles with central angle $\frac\pi4$.
Each has area $\frac12\cdot1\cdot1\cdot\sin\frac\pi4=\frac1{2\sqrt2}$, so these six give $6\cdot\frac1{2\sqrt2}=\frac3{\sqrt2}$.
The last side joins $e^{-i\pi/4}$ to $e^{i\pi/4}$ (the neighbours of the missing vertex $1$): central angle $\frac\pi2$, area $\frac12\cdot1\cdot1\cdot\sin\frac\pi2=\frac12$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Complement: regular octagon minus the corner triangle with vertices $e^{-i\pi/4},\,1,\,e^{i\pi/4}$.
solution: The regular octagon of circumradius $1$ has area $8\cdot\frac12\sin\frac\pi4=2\sqrt2$.
Removing the vertex $1$ cuts off the triangle with vertices $e^{-i\pi/4}$, $1$, $e^{i\pi/4}$.
Its base (the chord between $e^{\pm i\pi/4}$) is $\sqrt2$ and its height is $1-\cos\frac\pi4=1-\frac{\sqrt2}2$.

useful_results: $1+x+\dots+x^{n-1}=0\iff x^n=1,\ x\ne1$: the roots are the non-trivial $n$th roots of unity.
The $n$th roots of unity form a regular $n$-gon of area $\frac n2\sin\frac{2\pi}n$ (circumradius $1$); here $n=8$ gives $2\sqrt2$.
A polygon with one vertex removed is the full polygon minus the triangle on the two neighbours of that vertex.

concepts: Real and imaginary parts of $(a+ib)^3$
Integer solutions using prime factorisation
questions.question: If $a$ and $b$ are positive integers such that $N=(a+ib)^3-107i$ is a positive integer, find $N$.
questions.key_idea: $N$ real forces $\mathrm{Im}=3a^2b-b^3-107=0$, i.e. $b(3a^2-b^2)=107$ with $107$ prime.
solution: $N$ is a (real) integer, so the imaginary part vanishes: $3a^2b-b^3=107$, i.e. $b\left(3a^2-b^2\right)=107$.
$b=107$ would need $3a^2=1+107^2=11450$, which is not divisible by $3$ (digit sum $11$): impossible.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes b(3a^2-b^2)=107=107x1 and simply takes b=1. The other factorisation b=107 was not excluded; it is excluded now because 3a^2=11450 is not a multiple of 3. Answer unchanged.
useful_results: $(a+ib)^3=\left(a^3-3ab^2\right)+i\left(3a^2b-b^3\right)$.
A real-integer condition makes the imaginary part zero and turns the problem into a product of two integers equal to a prime: test only $1\cdot p$ and $p\cdot1$.

concepts: Conjugate roots of a real polynomial
Relations between roots and coefficients
questions.question: If the biquadratic $x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx+d=0$ ($a,b,c,d\in\mathbb R$) has $4$ non-real roots, two with sum $3+4i$ and the other two with product $13+i$, find the value of $b$.
questions.key_idea: A non-real sum means the two roots are not conjugates, so the other two roots are their conjugates; then $\alpha\beta=\overline{13+i}$.
solution: The polynomial is real with four non-real roots, so they form two conjugate pairs: roots $\alpha,\beta,\bar\alpha,\bar\beta$.
Take $\alpha+\beta=3+4i$ (non-real, so $\alpha,\beta$ are not conjugates of each other); the other two roots are then $\bar\alpha,\bar\beta$, and $\bar\alpha+\bar\beta=3-4i$.
$b=\sum$ of products of roots two at a time $=\alpha\beta+\alpha\bar\alpha+\alpha\bar\beta+\beta\bar\alpha+\beta\bar\beta+\bar\alpha\bar\beta$.
useful_results: Real polynomial: non-real roots occur in conjugate pairs; if two roots have a non-real sum they cannot be conjugates of each other, so the remaining two are their conjugates.
Coefficient of $x^2$ for roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$: $b=\alpha\beta+\gamma\delta+(\alpha+\beta)(\gamma+\delta)$.
Equivalent factor form: $\left(x^2-sx+p\right)\left(x^2-\bar sx+\bar p\right)$ with $s=3+4i$, $p=13-i$; its $x^2$ coefficient is $p+\bar p+|s|^2=26+25$.

concepts: Cube roots of unity and modulus
Integer solutions of a quadratic form
questions.question: If $\omega$ is the imaginary cube root of unity, find the number of ordered pairs of integers $(a,b)$ such that $|a\omega+b|=1$.
questions.key_idea: $|a\omega+b|^2=a^2-ab+b^2=(a-b)^2+ab$; integrality limits $(a-b)^2$ to $0$ or $1$.
solution: Let $m=(a-b)^2\ge0$ (a perfect square). Then $ab=1-m$ and $(a+b)^2=(a-b)^2+4ab=4-3m\ge0$, so $m\le\frac43$ and $m\in\{0,1\}$.
In all there are $2+4=6$ ordered pairs.
questions.correction_note: The PDF lists the cases (a-b)^2=0 and (a-b)^2=1 without proving that no other value of (a-b)^2 is possible. The bound (a+b)^2 = 4-3(a-b)^2 >= 0 was added to show the case list is complete. Answer 6 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: $a\omega+b$ is an Eisenstein integer of norm $a^2-ab+b^2$; norm $1$ means a unit, and there are exactly six units.
solution: The numbers $a\omega+b$ ($a,b\in\mathbb Z$) form a triangular lattice, and $|a\omega+b|^2=a^2-ab+b^2$.
In this lattice each point has exactly six nearest neighbours at distance $1$ from the origin: $\pm1,\ \pm\omega,\ \pm\omega^2$ (the sixth roots of unity).

useful_results: $|a+b\omega|^2=a^2-ab+b^2$ (norm form of Eisenstein integers), and $|a+b\omega+c\omega^2|^2=a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca$.
Completing the square, $a^2-ab+b^2=\left(a-\frac b2\right)^2+\frac34b^2=1$ gives $|b|\le\frac2{\sqrt3}$, so $|b|\le1$ (and likewise $|a|\le1$): only nine pairs to test.
Number of integer solutions of $a^2-ab+b^2=n$: $n=1$: $6$; $n=3$: $6$; $n=7$: $12$.

concepts: Loci in the Argand plane: half-plane, line and circle
questions.paragraph: Let $A,B,C$ be three sets of complex numbers as defined below: $A=\{z:\mathrm{Im}\,z\ge1\}$, $B=\{z:|z-2-i|=3\}$, $C=\{z:\mathrm{Re}\left((1-i)z\right)=\sqrt2\}$. [JEE-2008]
questions.question: The number of elements in the set $A\cap B\cap C$ is:
questions.key_idea: $C$ is the line $x+y=\sqrt2$ and $B$ a circle; the line cuts the circle in two points and $\mathrm{Im}\,z\ge1$ keeps only one.
solution: $B$: the circle $(x-2)^2+(y-1)^2=9$ (centre $(2,1)$, radius $3$). $A$: the closed half-plane $y\ge1$.
Intersect line and circle: put $x=\sqrt2-y$: $(y+2-\sqrt2)^2+(y-1)^2=9$, i.e. $y^2+(1-\sqrt2)y-(1+2\sqrt2)=0$.
Only $y\approx2.18\ge1$ lies in $A$; the other point has $y<1$.
So $A\cap B\cap C$ is a single point $S\approx(-0.76,\,2.18)$: the number of elements is $1$. Option (B).
questions.correction_note: The PDF says 'x=0, (y-1)^2=5, y=1+-sqrt5' and 'Only perpendicular point'. x=0 does not satisfy x+y=sqrt2 with those y (the point (0, 1+sqrt5) is not on the line), so that working is wrong. Correct: intersect x+y=sqrt2 with the circle, getting y=((sqrt2-1)+-sqrt(7+6 sqrt2))/2, and keep the root with y>=1. The count 1 and option (B) are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Count geometrically: the line meets the circle in a chord that crosses the line $y=1$ inside the circle, so exactly one end has $y>1$.
solution: The centre of $B$ is $(2,1)$; the distance to the line $x+y=\sqrt2$ is $\frac{|2+1-\sqrt2|}{\sqrt2}=\frac{3-\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}\approx1.12<3$, so the line cuts the circle in a chord.
The line meets $y=1$ at $(\sqrt2-1,\,1)$, at distance $2-(\sqrt2-1)=3-\sqrt2\approx1.59<3$ from the centre: this point lies inside the circle, on the chord.
So the chord crosses $y=1$ in its interior: one endpoint has $y>1$, the other $y<1$.
Only the endpoint with $y\ge1$ belongs to $A$, so $A\cap B\cap C$ has exactly $1$ element.

useful_results: $\mathrm{Re}\left[(1-i)z\right]=\sqrt2$ is the line $x+y=\sqrt2$; $\mathrm{Re}(\lambda z)=c$ is always a line.
Line versus circle: compare the distance from the centre with the radius; two intersection points if the distance is smaller.
A chord with an interior point on a horizontal line has its endpoints on opposite sides of it - this counts intersections with a half-plane without solving.

concepts: Loci in the Argand plane: circle and its diameter
questions.paragraph: Let $A,B,C$ be three sets of complex numbers as defined below: $A=\{z:\mathrm{Im}\,z\ge1\}$, $B=\{z:|z-2-i|=3\}$, $C=\{z:\mathrm{Re}\left((1-i)z\right)=\sqrt2\}$. [JEE-2008]
questions.question: Let $z$ be any point in $A\cap B\cap C$. Then $|z+1-i|^2+|z-5-i|^2$ lies between:
questions.key_idea: $-1+i$ and $5+i$ are the ends of a diameter of $B$, so the angle at $z$ is a right angle and Pythagoras applies.
solution: $z=S$ is the single point of $A\cap B\cap C$ found in Q23; it lies on the circle $B$ (centre $2+i$, radius $3$).
$|z+1-i|$ is the distance from $z$ to $P(-1,1)$ and $|z-5-i|$ is the distance from $z$ to $Q(5,1)$.
$P$ and $Q$ are at distance $3$ from the centre $(2,1)$ and on a horizontal line through it: they are the ends of a diameter of $B$, with $PQ=6$.
$S$ lies on the circle, so $\angle PSQ=90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle).

alternate_solutions.idea: Parallelogram law: $z+1-i=(z-2-i)+3$ and $z-5-i=(z-2-i)-3$.

useful_results: Parallelogram law: $|u+v|^2+|u-v|^2=2|u|^2+2|v|^2$.
For a point $X$ on the circle with diameter $PQ$: $XP^2+XQ^2=PQ^2$ (Thales + Pythagoras).
For any point $X$ with $M$ the midpoint of $PQ$: $XP^2+XQ^2=2XM^2+\frac12PQ^2$ (median theorem); on this circle $XM=3$ gives $18+18=36$.

concepts: Modulus and triangle inequality for complex numbers
questions.paragraph: Let $A,B,C$ be three sets of complex numbers as defined below: $A=\{z:\mathrm{Im}\,z\ge1\}$, $B=\{z:|z-2-i|=3\}$, $C=\{z:\mathrm{Re}\left((1-i)z\right)=\sqrt2\}$. [JEE-2008]
questions.question: Let $z$ be any point in $A\cap B\cap C$ and let $w$ be any point satisfying $|w-2-i|<3$. Then $|z|-|w|+3$ lies between:
questions.key_idea: 'Lies between' holds for every option whose interval contains the whole range; find the exact range from $|z|=|S|$ and $|w|\in[0,\sqrt5+3)$.
solution: $w$ lies inside the circle $B$ (centre $2+i$, radius $3$); $z=S$ lies on $B$, so $|z-w|<6$.
Hence $\left||z|-|w|\right|\le|z-w|<6$, i.e. $|z|-|w|\in(-6,6)$ and $|z|-|w|+3\in(-3,9)$ - this alone only supports (D).
'Lies between' is true for every option whose interval contains the whole set of values, so we need the exact range of $E=|z|-|w|+3$.
$S=(x,y)$ is on $x+y=\sqrt2$ and on the circle $(x-2)^2+(y-1)^2=9$, which gives $x^2+y^2=4x+2y+4$; so $|S|^2=3\sqrt2+5-\sqrt{7+6\sqrt2}\approx5.31$ and $|S|\approx2.30$.

questions.key_idea: Add $(1+x)^n$ at $x=1,\omega,\omega^2$: $1+\omega^r+\omega^{2r}$ is $3$ when $3\mid r$ and $0$ otherwise.
solution: Add (1)+(2)+(3): the coefficient of $C_r$ is $1+\omega^r+\omega^{2r}$, which is $3$ if $3\mid r$ and $0$ otherwise; so $2^n+(1+\omega)^n+(1+\omega^2)^n=3\left(C_0+C_3+C_6+\dots\right)$.

solution: Only (B) survives. (Option elimination - the derivation above proves it.)

$1+\omega^r+\omega^{2r}=3$ if $3\mid r$, else $0$; and $1+\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, $1+\omega^2=e^{-i\pi/3}$ give the $\cos\frac{n\pi}3$.

questions.question:
Match the statements given in Column I with the values given in Column II. [JEE-2011]

Column I
(A) If $\vec a=\hat j+\sqrt3\hat k$, $\vec b=-\hat j+\sqrt3\hat k$ and $\vec c=2\sqrt3\hat k$ form a triangle, then the internal angle of the triangle between $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ is:
(B) If $\int_a^b\left(f(x)-3x\right)dx=a^2-b^2$, then the value of $f\left(\frac\pi6\right)$ is:
(C) The value of $\frac{\pi^2}{\ln3}\int_{7/6}^{5/6}\sec(\pi x)\,dx$ is:
(D) The maximum value of $\left|\mathrm{Arg}\left(\frac1{1-z}\right)\right|$ for $|z|=1,\ z\ne1$ is given by:

Column II
(p) $\frac\pi6$   (q) $\frac{2\pi}3$   (r) $\frac\pi3$   (s) $\pi$   (t) $\frac\pi2$
questions.key_idea: Each part has one trap: the interior angle is $\pi$ minus the vector angle; $\int_a^bg$ known for all $a,b$ means differentiate; reversed limits; $\left|\mathrm{Arg}\right|$ only approaches $\frac\pi2$.
solution: (A) $\vec a\cdot\vec b=-1+3=2$ and $|\vec a|=|\vec b|=2$, so the angle between the vectors is $\theta$ with $\cos\theta=\frac24=\frac12$, $\theta=\frac\pi3$.

Here $\vec c=\vec a+\vec b$ (lengths $2,2,2\sqrt3$), so $\vec a,\vec b$ are the sides taken head to tail; the interior angle between them is $\pi-\frac\pi3=\frac{2\pi}3$, opposite the longest side. (A)$\to$(q).
(B) $\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=\frac32\left(b^2-a^2\right)+a^2-b^2=\frac{b^2-a^2}2$ for all $a,b$; differentiating w.r.t. $b$ gives $f(b)=b$, so $f(x)=x$ and $f\left(\frac\pi6\right)=\frac\pi6$. (B)$\to$(p).

(C) $\int\sec(\pi x)\,dx=\frac1\pi\ln\left|\sec\pi x+\tan\pi x\right|$. At $x=\frac56$: $\sec=-\frac2{\sqrt3}$, $\tan=-\frac1{\sqrt3}$, so $\left|\sec+\tan\right|=\sqrt3$; at $x=\frac76$: $\sec=-\frac2{\sqrt3}$, $\tan=\frac1{\sqrt3}$, so the value is $\frac1{\sqrt3}$.
(D) Let $u=\frac1{1-z}$, so $z=1-\frac1u$ and $|z|=1$ gives $\left|1-\frac1u\right|=1$, i.e. $|u-1|=|u|$: $u$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $0$ and $1$, $\mathrm{Re}\,u=\frac12$.

On this line $\mathrm{Arg}\,u$ takes every value in $\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$; $\left|\mathrm{Arg}\,u\right|$ approaches $\frac\pi2$ but never attains it ($u\to\infty$ means $z\to1$), so the supremum is $\frac\pi2$. (D)$\to$(t).

alternate_solutions.idea: A quicker check for each part: cosine rule on sides $2,2,2\sqrt3$; differentiate in $b$; use that $\sec$ is even after $x=1+t$; write $z=e^{i\theta}$.
solution: (A) The sides have lengths $|\vec a|=|\vec b|=2$ and $|\vec c|=2\sqrt3$. By the cosine rule the angle between the two equal sides satisfies $\cos\gamma=\frac{4+4-12}{2\cdot2\cdot2}=-\frac12$, so $\gamma=\frac{2\pi}3$ - no head-to-tail confusion. (q)
(C) Put $x=1+t$: $\sec(\pi+\pi t)=-\sec\pi t$ and $t$ runs from $\frac16$ to $-\frac16$, so the integral equals $\int_{-1/6}^{1/6}\sec\pi t\,dt=2\int_0^{1/6}\sec\pi t\,dt$ (even integrand).

Its argument is $\tan^{-1}\left(\cot\frac\theta2\right)=\frac\pi2-\frac\theta2\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$; $|\mathrm{Arg}|$ comes arbitrarily close to $\frac\pi2$ as $\theta\to0^+$ or $2\pi^-$ but never reaches it: supremum $\frac\pi2$. (t)

If $\int_a^bg\,dx=F(b)-F(a)$ holds for all $a,b$, differentiate: $g(b)=F'(b)$.
$\int\sec\theta\,d\theta=\ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|$; $\sec$ is even, so symmetric limits double the half-integral.

For $|z|=1$, $z\ne1$: $\frac1{1-z}=\frac12+\frac i2\cot\frac\theta2$ lies on the line $\mathrm{Re}=\frac12$ and its argument fills $(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2)$ - the 'maximum' $\frac\pi2$ is a supremum, not attained.

questions.key_idea: Four short computations: $\frac{2iz}{1-z^2}=-\frac1y$ on the unit circle; the $\sin^{-1}$ argument is $\frac{8t}{9-t^2}$ with $t=3^x$; the determinant is $2\sec^2\theta$; $f'=\frac{15}2\sqrt x(x-2)$.
solution: (A) Let $z=x+iy$, $x^2+y^2=1$, so $1-x^2=y^2$, and $z\ne\pm1$ means $y\ne0$. Then $1-z^2=(1-x^2+y^2)-2ixy=2y^2-2ixy=2y(y-ix)$ and $2iz=2(ix-y)=-2(y-ix)$.
So $\frac{2iz}{1-z^2}=\frac{-2(y-ix)}{2y(y-ix)}=-\frac1y$, which is real, with $0<|y|\le1$; hence the set is $(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)$. (A)$\to$(s).
(B) Need $-1\le\frac{8\cdot3^{x-2}}{1-3^{2(x-1)}}\le1$ with $x\ne1$. Let $t=3^x>0$: $3^{x-2}=\frac t9$ and $3^{2(x-1)}=\frac{t^2}9$, so the expression is $\frac{8t}{9-t^2}$, $t\ne3$.
Case $0<t<3$ ($9-t^2>0$): the lower bound is automatic; $\frac{8t}{9-t^2}\le1\Rightarrow t^2+8t-9\le0\Rightarrow(t+9)(t-1)\le0\Rightarrow t\le1\Rightarrow x\le0$.
Case $t>3$ ($9-t^2<0$): the upper bound is automatic; $\frac{8t}{9-t^2}\ge-1\Rightarrow t^2-8t-9\ge0\Rightarrow(t-9)(t+1)\ge0\Rightarrow t\ge9\Rightarrow x\ge2$.

(C) Apply $R_1\to R_1+R_3$: the first row becomes $(0,\ 0,\ 2)$. Expand along it: $f(\theta)=2\left|\begin{matrix}-\tan\theta&1\\-1&-\tan\theta\end{matrix}\right|=2\left(\tan^2\theta+1\right)=2\sec^2\theta$.
For $0\le\theta<\frac\pi2$, $\sec^2\theta$ takes all values in $[1,\infty)$, so the set is $[2,\infty)$. (C)$\to$(r).
$f'(x)\ge0$ for $x\ge2$ and $f'<0$ on $(0,2)$, so $f$ is increasing in $[2,\infty)$. (D)$\to$(r).
